a: A segmentation fault means your program touched memory it should not, usually in C or C++: a bad pointer, an array out of range, or use after free. Compile with -g and run in gdb or use valgrind to find the line.
more: In higher level languages this shows up as an index or null error instead.

a: You have infinite or too deep recursion. Every call needs a base case that stops it, and each call must move toward that base case.
more: Convert deep recursion to a loop if the depth can be huge.

a: An infinite loop means the stop condition never becomes false. Check that the loop variable changes every pass and that your condition is right. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.
more: Add a print inside the loop to see the values change.

a: You are calling something that is not a function. Check spelling, that the import worked, and that the value is not undefined. console.log(typeof thing) shows what it really is.
more: Often caused by a wrong import or calling a method on the wrong object.

a: Node cannot find that package or file. Run npm install, check the package name, and for your own files check the path starts with ./ and the filename is exact.
more: Case matters on Linux servers like Render.

a: A ReferenceError means you used a name that does not exist in this scope. Check for typos, a missing let/const, or code that runs before the variable is created.
more: In browsers, scripts also fail if the file loads after the code that needs it.

a: JSON.parse got empty or broken text. Log the raw response first. The server may have returned HTML, an error page, or nothing. Also check for trailing commas and single quotes.
more: Use response.ok before calling response.json().

a: The request never reached a server. Common causes: wrong URL, server down, no internet, blocked by CORS, or mixed http and https. Check the Network tab in browser dev tools.
more: If it works in Postman but not the browser, it is almost always CORS.

a: KeyError means that key is not in the dictionary. Use d.get('key') for a default, or check with if 'key' in d first.
more: Print d.keys() to see what you actually have.

a: You asked for a position that does not exist. Lists start at 0 and the last valid index is len(list)-1. Check the list is not empty and that your loop does not run too far.
more: Off-by-one errors are the most common cause.

a: ValueError means the type is right but the value is not, like int('abc'). Validate input first or wrap the call in try/except ValueError.
more: input() always returns text, convert it on purpose.

a: Python does not know that name. You may have a typo, forgot to define or import it, or used it before the line that creates it.
more: Variable names are case sensitive.

a: You mixed types, like adding a string and a number. Convert first: str(5) or int('5'), or use an f-string: f'Age: {age}'.
more: print(type(x)) tells you what you really have.

a: You divided by 0. Check the divisor before dividing: if b != 0. In JavaScript you get Infinity instead of an error.
more: Handle it explicitly rather than hiding it.

a: Your user is not allowed to do that. Check the file permissions with ls -l, use chmod to fix them, or run the command as the right user. With npm, avoid sudo and fix the global folder instead.
more: Never chmod 777 on a server.

q: is not recognized as an internal or external command
a: The terminal cannot find that program. It is not installed, or its folder is not in your PATH. Install it, then restart the terminal.
more: On Windows, reinstall and tick Add to PATH.

a: npm cannot find that script in package.json. Open it and add the script inside "scripts", for example "start": "node server.js".
more: npm run lists the scripts you have.

a: Your remote has commits you do not have. Run git pull --rebase (or git pull), fix any conflicts, then push again. Do not force push on shared branches.
more: git status shows where you stand.

a: Detached HEAD means you checked out a commit instead of a branch. To keep your work run git switch -c new-branch-name. To go back run git switch main.
more: Commits made while detached are lost if you do not save them to a branch.

a: 401 means the server does not know who you are, so check your login or token. 403 means it knows you but you are not allowed, so check permissions and roles.
more: Check you sent the Authorization header correctly.

a: 502 and 504 mean the server in front could not get a good answer from your app, often because it crashed or is too slow. 503 means it is overloaded or restarting. Check your app logs and whether it starts correctly.
more: On free hosts, a sleeping app can return 503 for the first request.

a: The server did not answer in time. Check the URL and port, your firewall, whether the server is running, and add retries with a sensible timeout.
more: A firewall dropping traffic often looks like a timeout.

a: Your program used more memory than allowed. Process data in chunks or streams, free big objects you no longer need, and look for lists that grow forever. Node: node --max-old-space-size=4096.
more: A memory leak is usually something stored in a global that never gets cleared.

a: An off-by-one error is when a loop runs one time too many or too few. Remember that arrays start at 0, and decide whether your end is inclusive or exclusive.
more: Test with the smallest and largest inputs.

a: Your browser is probably using a cached copy. Hard refresh with Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on Mac), or open dev tools and tick Disable cache. Also confirm you saved the file and deployed.
more: Add a version query like style.css?v=2 to force a refresh.

a: Open the deploy logs and read the first red error, not the last. Common causes: wrong start command, missing dependency in package.json, wrong Node version, or the app not listening on process.env.PORT.
more: Make sure the file names match exactly, Linux is case sensitive.

a: Another program is using that port. Stop it, or start yours on another port. Mac/Linux: lsof -i :3000 shows the process, then kill it. Windows: netstat -ano | findstr :3000.
more: Sometimes it is just your old server still running in another terminal.

a: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser so you can build servers. npm is its package manager.
CORS is a browser rule that blocks a page from calling a different domain unless that server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers.

q: what is cannot read property of undefined
a: You are using a value that is undefined. Check the variable is set before use, log it, and use optional chaining like obj?.name.
A syntax error means the code breaks the language rules, usually a missing bracket, quote, comma or colon near the line it reports.
Python uses indentation to group code. Use 4 spaces consistently and never mix tabs and spaces.
Python cannot find that library. Install it with pip install name, and make sure you are in the right virtual environment.
404 means the server has no page at that URL. Check the spelling, the route and that the file is deployed.
500 means the server crashed while handling the request. Check the server logs for the real error message.
EADDRINUSE means that port is taken by another program. Stop the other process or run on a different port.
A virtual environment is an isolated Python setup per project so libraries do not clash. Create one with python -m venv venv.
pip installs Python libraries, for example pip install requests.
